Lost in translation

In puzzle 5, Swift saw your Kotlin through an Objective-C header. Objective-C is simpler than both languages, so some things don't make it across. Here are the three that bite.

The problem

In puzzle 5, Swift reached your Kotlin through an Objective-C header. Your shared code returns a Flow<User>, has suspend functions, and throws an IOException when the login fails. The generated header has to describe all three using Objective-C. What can it express at that boundary?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Start with the value. Compare a flow of users with a flow of orders. Could a Swift caller distinguish them from the types in the generated header alone?

Generics. Objective-C allows type parameters only on classes, not on interfaces. Kotlin's Flow is an interface, so Flow<User> arrives in Swift without its User: Swift sees "some Flow" and has to be told what's inside. A class like Box<User> keeps its User.

Now keep the result type fixed. Imagine a function returning a single user. If that user arrives later, how does the caller learn the result is ready?

suspend functions. Objective-C has no coroutines. Its way of saying "later" is a completion handler: a function you pass in, which is called with the result when it's ready. So each suspend function becomes a method that takes a completion handler. Swift has its own version of suspend: an async function, which the caller waits for with await, without blocking, much as a coroutine waits at a suspend call. Swift 5.5 and later can also expose an async form for the imported Kotlin function. The completion handler is the underlying interface. This bridge has limitations, so test the generated interface you ship.

Finally, keep the timing fixed. Imagine an ordinary function that either returns the user immediately or throws IOException. Which failure did the generated header promise Swift could handle?

Exceptions. Every Kotlin exception is unchecked: nothing forces the caller to handle it. Swift's errors are checked: a function that can fail says so with throws, and the caller must handle it. For this bridge, list the expected exceptions with @Throws. Those classes and their subclasses reach Swift as errors it can catch. An unexpected exception escaping the bridge can terminate the app. If a suspending function is asked to stop, it can pass the error that signals this even without @Throws.

None of this is a bug: it's the price of the bridge from puzzle 5. Knowing it lets you shape your API so Swift gets what it needs: generic classes instead of generic interfaces, and a deliberate error contract for functions you expose.

The analogy

The translation from puzzle 5 again. A word the third language doesn't have (a Kotlin interface's type parameter) is dropped. An idiom it can't express ("suspend") is rewritten into a phrase it has ("call me back"). And a warning nobody translated (an unlisted exception) reaches the reader as silence, then a crash.

Check yourself

Your shared code exposes a Flow<User>. What does Swift see?

Not quite. Generics cross only on classes; Flow is an interface, so its type parameter is lost.

Right. Interface generics are lost in the Objective-C header.

Not quite. The Flow does cross, as an Objective-C type; only its type parameter is lost.

An ordinary Kotlin function throws IOException and has no @Throws. Swift calls it, and it throws. What happens?

Not quite. Only exceptions listed in @Throws become Swift errors; the rest end the app.

Right. For ordinary functions, the annotation declares errors that may cross the bridge.

Not quite. Nothing catches it on the way; an unlisted exception ends the app.

What's the difference between a suspend function in Kotlin and what Swift sees?

Right. Suspend becomes "call me back when done".

Not quite. Nothing blocks: the completion handler is called later, with the result.

Not quite. Swift has no suspend; Objective-C's bridge turns it into a completion handler.

Sources
  • Kotlin docs: Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C ("Generics can only be defined on classes, not on interfaces (protocols in Objective-C and Swift) or functions"; mapping table: "suspend → completionHandler: / async"; "All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked… Swift has only checked errors"; "Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination")

What you now know

Through the Objective-C header, generics on interfaces are lost (a Flow<User> arrives without its User), suspend functions become completion handlers (async in Swift), and an unexpected Kotlin exception escaping the bridge can terminate the app.
